Intussusception is rare under 3 months and exceedingly rare under 6 weeks; absence of currant-jelly stool or palpable mass further reduces likelihood. Sweat chloride is appropriately flagged as *consider*—not urgent—supporting that CF/meconium ileus is secondary in suspicion.

- Infant aged <1 month (implied by “young infant” + presentation at 3–4 days)  
- Progressive irritability and poor feeding over 3–4 days  
- Marked abdominal tenderness on palpation  
- Abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops  
- Abdominal X-ray shows absence of rectal gas  
- Normal CBC (no leukocytosis, no anemia, no thrombocytopenia) — argues against sepsis/inflammation  
- No fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or systemic illness reported  
- Key impression includes “suspected mechanical intestinal obstruction” with Hirschsprung disease listed first among differentials  
- Contrast enema recommended specifically for “aganglionosis evaluation”

- Gestational age (to distinguish preterm vs. term — affects timing of meconium passage and HD presentation)  
- History of meconium passage (e.g., delayed/absent meconium in first 48h — highly supportive of HD or meconium ileus)  
- Physical exam findings: presence/absence of abdominal distension, palpable stool mass, or empty rectal vault on digital exam  
- Contrast enema results (to confirm transition zone or megacolon)  
- Rectal biopsy result (gold standard for HD)  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Hirschsprung disease
